title: A real friend
hookLine: a friend isn't the one who says 'I'm your friend'; it's the one who stands by you
carry: a child asleep on a parent's chest

lines: A DOZEN SAID YES. TWO CAME.
cards: You're moving apartments. Forty boxes, a couch, a Saturday in August. In the group chat, a dozen people said, of course, anything you need!
At eight in the morning, two of them show up. Those two are the ones the day belongs to. A few weeks ago, the advice to Sigala gave a way to tell true friends from false ones.
The third poem of this chapter is shorter and sharper: five verses about the gap between saying and doing.

teach.h: I'M YOUR FRIEND, BUT NO HELP
teach.b: The poem is called the Hiri Sutta, after the word it begins with: hiri, a sense of shame, a conscience. It starts with someone who has none, who says I'm your friend, but never takes on any task they could easily do.
Know them, the poem says: they're not my friend. Then: someone who speaks pleasant words to friends but doesn't follow through.
The wise see that person clearly: all talk, no doing. Then a surprise.
It's also not a friend who is always on alert for a break, watching you for faults, keeping score. Friendship that's suspicious is its own kind of failure. And then the picture of the real thing.

teach.h: A CHILD ASLEEP ON A PARENT'S CHEST
teach.b: A real friend is the one you can rest on, the poem says, like a child asleep on a parent's chest. Someone others can't split you away from. Stay with that image.
A child on a parent's chest doesn't check, doesn't wonder whether it's safe, doesn't earn its place. It just rests.
That's what being a real friend makes possible for someone else. And it's built by deeds, not speeches: showing up, doing the task you could do, not keeping a list of the other person's mistakes.
The poem's last verses turn inward, to the quiet joy of a good life and of the teaching. As if to say: the kind of person who can be that friend is someone at peace enough not to need the credit.

how: Buddhist teachers read the Hiri Sutta alongside the advice to Sigala on true and false friends, as practical guidance for lay friendship.

o: a business partner bound by a contract
a relative you must always obey
a friend: the one who does, not just says

games.q: a real friend: tap the pairs.
p: but does no task they could
like a child asleep on a parent's chest

s: the poem says a friend who's always watching you for faults is not a real friend
suspicious score-keeping is its own failure of friendship.
in the poem, saying I'm your friend is enough
the friend who says it but does no task they could is not a friend.
the poem's picture of real friendship is a child resting on a parent's chest
someone you can rest on, whom others can't split you from.

games.q: a friend is moving and asks for help. you said 'anything you need!' in the group chat. what does the poem count?
o: showing up and doing the task you could do.
how often you check whether they helped you.
games.why: the poem judges friendship by deeds: whoever says I'm your friend but takes on no task they could is not a friend.

practice: Think of someone who could use a friend to rest on right now, someone moving, grieving, overwhelmed or just quiet lately, and picture what would actually help: not let me know if you need anything, but one specific thing.
Then let go of any score you've been keeping with them, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Mitta, friend. Not the one who says I'm your friend, but the one who does the task, doesn't keep score, and can be rested on like a parent's chest. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali mitta (Sanskrit mitra): friend. the root of metta, loving-kindness.

carryVoice: Your line: a child asleep on a parent's chest. The kind of friend someone can rest on. That's day five hundred ninety-two.
